554.title: More blessed to give (Acts 20:17–38)
554.hook: Paul's farewell at Miletus; they weep and kneel on the shore
554.howItsDone: Catholics practice almsgiving, one of the three traditional disciplines of Lent alongside prayer and fasting, and give to the poor through parish collections and works of mercy throughout the year.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Eutychus, asleep in the window while Paul talked till dawn. Your line was even Paul went on.

A beach at Miletus, on the coast of Asia. Paul is in a hurry to reach Jerusalem, so he doesn't go up to Ephesus, where he spent about three years. Instead he sends for the elders of the Ephesian church, and they make the journey down to the shore. He tells them plainly: I don't know what will happen to me in Jerusalem, except that prison and hardship are waiting. And you will not see my face again.
screen: `A BEACH AT MILETUS.` → `THE ELDERS OF EPHESUS.` → `YOU WILL NOT SEE MY FACE AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Paul's farewell sounds like a man setting his affairs in order. He reminds them how he lived among them: serving the Lord with humility and tears, holding nothing back, teaching in public and from house to house. He tells them to keep watch over the flock, like shepherds. Then he holds up his hands. I've coveted no one's silver or gold or clothing. These hands, he says, worked for my own needs and for those who were with me. Then he gives them a saying of Jesus, in the Douay-Rheims: "remember the word of the Lord Jesus, how he said: It is a more blessed thing to give, rather than to receive." Here's the surprise: those words of Jesus aren't in any of the four Gospels. Matthew, Mark, Luke and John never record them. It's a saying of Jesus preserved only here, in Paul's mouth, passed along by Luke, kept by people who remembered it. And Paul isn't asking the elders for money. He's showing them his own work-worn hands and saying: this is how to lead. Give. Then the ending. Paul kneels down on the shore and prays with them all. They weep, embrace him, and kiss him, grieving most of all, the text says, because he told them they would not see his face again. And they walk him to the ship.

segments.voice: Look at your hands, the way Paul held up his, and ask what they've given lately. Think of one thing you could give freely, without being asked, not necessarily money: time, a meal, a compliment you meant to say, help with a task, something you own that someone else needs more, and picture handing it over without waiting for thanks. If you pray, offer your hands for whatever giving the day brings.

555.title: Arrested (Acts 21–22)
555.hook: a riot in the Temple and Paul tells his own story
555.howItsDone: In Catholic parishes, adults entering the Church often share their faith story with sponsors and the community during their preparation, and Catholics speak of giving witness by telling plainly what God has done in their lives.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the farewell on the beach at Miletus. Your line was coveted no one's silver.

Paul reaches Jerusalem. Friends along the way had begged him not to go. A prophet named Agabus even tied his own hands and feet with Paul's belt to show what was coming. Paul went anyway. In Jerusalem, James and the elders welcome him, and to show he still honors the Law, Paul goes to the Temple to be purified with four men under a vow. He's a Jew, worshiping in the Temple of his people. And that's where it all breaks loose.
screen: `AGABUS AND THE BELT.` → `PAUL GOES ANYWAY.` → `TO THE TEMPLE, TO KEEP A VOW.`

segments.voice: Some visitors from Asia see Paul in the Temple and shout that he has brought Greeks into the holy place. He hadn't. They'd seen him in the city earlier with Trophimus, a Gentile from Ephesus, and assumed. The crowd seizes Paul, drags him out, and the gates are shut. They're trying to kill him when word reaches the Roman commander of the garrison, who runs down with soldiers. The beating stops. Paul is chained and carried up the steps of the barracks, the crowd is so violent. At the top of the steps, bruised and in chains, Paul asks to speak. The commander is surprised he speaks Greek. Paul says he is a Jew of Tarsus in Cilicia, in the Douay-Rheims, "a citizen of no mean city." Then he turns and speaks to the crowd in their own language, Hebrew or Aramaic, and they fall quiet. What does he say? Not an argument. His story. I was brought up in this city at the feet of Gamaliel. I persecuted this Way. On the road to Damascus a light shone around me, and I heard a voice: "Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?" Then a devout man named Ananias came and said, Brother Saul, look up. That's all: what happened to him. They listen, until he says the Lord sent him to the Gentiles. Then the uproar starts again. Later, about to be flogged, Paul quietly asks the centurion whether it's lawful to scourge a Roman citizen who hasn't been condemned. It isn't. The flogging stops.

segments.voice: If someone asked why you're on this path, practicing, listening, whatever brought you here, what would you say? Not an argument, just what happened: who you were before, one moment that changed something, where you are now, in three short sentences in your head. It doesn't have to be dramatic, and if you pray, thank God for one moment in it.

556.title: Almost (Acts 26)
556.hook: King Agrippa says almost thou persuadest me
556.howItsDone: Catholics are encouraged to examine their consciences regularly, often at night, noticing what they have left undone as well as done, and many bring those things to the sacrament of reconciliation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Paul arrested in the Temple, telling his story from the barracks steps. Your line was tell what happened.

Two years pass. Paul sits in custody in Caesarea, on the coast, while governors come and go. Then a new governor, Festus, gets a royal visit: King Agrippa and Bernice arrive with great pomp, the text says, with commanders and the city's leading men. Festus has a prisoner he doesn't know what to do with, and the king is curious. So Paul is brought in, in chains, to a hall full of power, and invited to speak.
screen: `TWO YEARS IN CAESAREA.` → `A KING ARRIVES WITH GREAT POMP.` → `A PRISONER IN A HALL OF POWER.`

segments.voice: Paul tells it again: the road, the light at midday brighter than the sun, the voice. This time he includes a line he hasn't mentioned before. The voice said, in the Douay-Rheims, "It is hard for thee to kick against the goad," like an ox kicking the stick that steers it. Paul had been fighting what was pulling him. He tells how he was sent to open eyes and turn people from darkness to light. Festus can't take it. He shouts: "Paul, thou art beside thyself: much learning doth make thee mad." Paul answers calmly, I am not mad, most noble Festus. Then he turns to the king. King Agrippa, do you believe the prophets? I know you do. And Agrippa replies, in the Douay-Rheims: "In a little thou persuadest me to become a Christian." The King James turns that into almost, today's word. And there's Antioch's word, Christian, in a king's mouth. What did Agrippa mean? Honestly, nobody's sure. The Greek is two short words, en oligo, in a little. It could mean almost, or in such a short time, or with so little effort. He might be moved; he might be brushing Paul off with a smile. Paul's answer works either way: I would to God that, in a little and in much, not only you but all who hear me today might become such as I am, "except these bands." Picture him raising his chained hands. Then the king rises, and the hearing is over. This man could have gone free, Agrippa remarks, if he hadn't appealed to Caesar. So to Rome he goes.

557.title: Shipwreck (Acts 27–28:10)
557.hook: a storm, a wreck, everyone saved, and a viper on Malta
557.howItsDone: In Malta, the feast of Saint Paul's Shipwreck on February 10 is a public holiday with Mass and a procession, and Catholics there honor Paul as the island's father in faith.

segments.voice: Yesterday, King Agrippa's slippery answer to Paul. Your line was kick against the goad.

Acts 27 reads like a sea novel, told in the first person plural: we set sail, we were driven, we were cast ashore. The narrator was on board. Paul is a prisoner bound for Rome under a centurion named Julius. It's late in the sailing season, and Paul warns them this voyage will bring damage and loss. The ship's master and owner want to push on to a better harbor, and the centurion listens to them, not to the prisoner. A gentle south wind blows. They set out. Then a violent northeaster comes down off the island of Crete.
screen: `WE SET SAIL: THE NARRATOR WAS ON BOARD.` → `PAUL WARNS THEM.` → `THE NORTHEASTER HITS.`

segments.voice: The ship can't face the wind, so they let it drive them. They throw cargo overboard, then the ship's tackle. For many days neither sun nor stars appear, and all hope of being saved, the text says, was taken away. Then Paul stands up among them. Be of good cheer, he says; an angel of God stood by me tonight: not one life will be lost, only the ship. On the fourteenth night, near land, Paul urges everyone to eat, and says, in the Douay-Rheims: "for there shall not an hair of the head of any of you perish." He takes bread, gives thanks to God in front of them all, breaks it, and begins to eat. And everyone eats: two hundred seventy-six people, Luke counts. At daylight they run the ship aground and it breaks apart. The soldiers plan to kill the prisoners so none escape, but the centurion, wanting to save Paul, stops them. Swimmers swim, the rest float on planks, and, the text says, they all got safe to land. The island is Malta. The islanders show them unusual kindness and light a fire in the rain. Paul gathers a bundle of sticks, and a viper comes out from the heat and fastens on his hand. A murderer, the islanders say; justice won't let him live. Paul shakes it into the fire and nothing happens. They wait for him to swell up. When he doesn't, they change their minds and say he's a god. Luke tells it with a straight face. Malta still keeps the feast of Saint Paul's Shipwreck every February tenth.

segments.voice: Think of a place where people around you are anxious: a family worry, a shaky job, a friend in a storm. Paul didn't pretend the storm was small; he ate, gave thanks, and helped others eat, so picture yourself as the steady one in that room, with a slow breath, a plain kind word, maybe a meal. If you pray, pray for the people in your boat.

558.title: Rome, unhindered (Acts 28:30–31)
558.hook: Paul under house arrest, welcoming all, preaching with confidence
558.howItsDone: Catholics celebrate Saints Peter and Paul together on June 29, and pilgrims to Rome visit Paul's tomb at the Basilica of Saint Paul Outside the Walls, on the road to Ostia.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the shipwreck, and every soul brought safe to Malta. Your line was not a hair shall perish.

A prisoner walks toward the capital of the world, as Luke's readers knew it. Back on day five hundred thirty-four, at the very start of Acts, Jesus told his friends they would be his witnesses in Jerusalem, in Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth. Since then the story has gone out of the upper room, through Samaria and the desert road, to Antioch, across the sea to Philippi, Athens and Corinth, and through a shipwreck. Now it reaches Rome, and Paul walks in as a prisoner.
screen: `JERUSALEM, JUDEA, SAMARIA.` → `ANTIOCH, PHILIPPI, ATHENS.` → `AND NOW, ROME.`

segments.voice: As Paul nears the city on the Appian Way, believers from Rome walk out to meet him, at the Forum of Appius and the Three Taverns. When Paul saw them, Luke says, he thanked God and took courage. Even an apostle needed friends to show up. In Rome he's allowed to live by himself, with a soldier guarding him. He calls together the leaders of the Jewish community and speaks with them all day, from morning to evening. Some are persuaded, some are not, and they leave still discussing among themselves. Then come the last two verses of the book, in the Douay-Rheims: "And he remained two whole years in his own hired lodging; and he received all that came in to him, Preaching the kingdom of God, and teaching the things which concern the Lord Jesus Christ, with all confidence, without prohibition." That's how Acts ends. Not with Paul's trial. Not with his death. The Douay says without prohibition; the last word in the Greek, akolutos, means unhindered, without hindrance. A man in chains, renting a room, opening his door to whoever comes, and the word is not chained. Why does Luke stop there? Nobody knows for certain. Maybe he wrote before the trial ended. Maybe he wanted the story to stay open, because it isn't finished. Catholic tradition holds that Paul was later martyred in Rome under Nero and buried on the road to Ostia, where the Basilica of Saint Paul Outside the Walls now stands. Acts itself doesn't tell it.

segments.voice: Paul couldn't go anywhere, so he let the world come to him. Picture your own small room, your desk, your kitchen, your phone, and who might come through it: an unexpected call, a neighbor, a coworker with a question, a kid with a long story; picture receiving them the way Paul received all that came in, with the door open. If you pray, thank God for the friends who walked out to meet you when you needed it.
Rome. Where Acts ends, with Paul in a rented room, welcoming everyone, preaching without hindrance. Today's word.

Your line: without hindrance. And that's the Acts of the Apostles: witnesses, Pentecost, deacons, the road to Damascus, the council, Lydia, the jail, Athens, the shipwreck, and Rome. Tomorrow, the letters.

559.title: How Paul wrote
559.hook: letters dictated to real churches with real problems, before the gospels were written
559.howItsDone: At Sunday Mass, Catholics usually hear three readings, and the second is most often from the New Testament letters, many of them Paul's; it is read aloud to the whole assembly, as the letters first were.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rome, and Acts ending on the word unhindered. Your line was without hindrance.

A box of old family letters, found in an attic. Not speeches. Letters. Answers to questions nobody wrote down, jokes that need context, names no one remembers, a worry about money, a fight between cousins, and then, in the middle of it all, a paragraph worth reading twice. That's what i'm opening today: a new part of the path, the letters of the New Testament, and first, the letters of Paul.
screen: `A BOX OF OLD LETTERS.` → `QUESTIONS WE CAN'T SEE.` → `A NEW PART: THE LETTERS.`

segments.voice: The word is epistle, from the Greek epistole: simply a letter, something sent. First surprise: a common scholarly view places Paul's letters before the Gospels were written down. On that view, opening Paul means hearing a voice from the first Christian generation, writing to churches that were still new. Second, Paul didn't always hold the pen. At times he dictated to a secretary, and at the end of Romans the secretary slips in his own greeting. In the Douay-Rheims: "I Tertius, who wrote this epistle, salute you in the Lord." In several letters Paul then takes the pen for the last lines, as a signature. To the Galatians: "See what a letter I have written to you with my own hand." The Greek speaks of large letters: big handwriting, his own. Third, these were real letters to real people with real problems. Corinth is split into factions. The Galatians are confused. The Thessalonians are grieving their dead. Paul answers them, scolds them, misses them, and greets friends by name. The letters were carried by hand and read aloud to the whole church. A whole set of New Testament letters carries Paul's name. Scholars debate whether he wrote every one or whether some come from his close followers; the Church receives all of them as scripture. At Sunday Mass, the second reading often comes from these letters. You're hearing someone else's mail, and it was meant to be shared.
screen: `EPISTOLE: A LETTER, SOMETHING SENT.` · `LIKELY BEFORE THE GOSPELS.` · `DICTATED, THEN SIGNED IN BIG LETTERS.` · `REAL CHURCHES, REAL PROBLEMS.` · then, large: `READ ALOUD TO EVERYONE.`

560.title: Not ashamed (Romans 1:16)
560.hook: the gospel is the power of God unto salvation
560.howItsDone: Many Catholics make the sign of the cross and say grace before meals, including in public, and at Mass they trace a small cross on the forehead, lips and heart before the Gospel is read.

segments.voice: Yesterday, how Paul wrote: dictated letters, signed in big handwriting. Your line was real letters to real people.

A restaurant table, coworkers all around, plates arriving. Someone wonders whether to make the sign of the cross before eating, and doesn't. Someone else is asked about Sunday and says, oh, not much. Nobody is persecuting anyone. It's just easier not to mention it. The letter that stands first among the New Testament's letters takes up that small hesitation in its very first chapter.
screen: `THE SIGN OF THE CROSS AT LUNCH?` → `OH, NOT MUCH.` → `ROMANS, CHAPTER ONE.`

segments.voice: Romans is a letter to a church Paul had not founded and had never visited. He's writing ahead, probably from Corinth, introducing himself before he arrives. It comes first among the letters in your Bible, but it isn't the oldest: Paul's letters are arranged roughly by length, longest first. Near the start, Paul says what the whole letter is about. In the Douay-Rheims: "For I am not ashamed of the gospel. For it is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth, to the Jew first, and to the Greek." Why mention shame at all? Because in his world, his message was embarrassing. Crucifixion was a death meant to disgrace, used on slaves and rebels. God's anointed one dying on a cross sounded absurd to outsiders, as Paul admits in another letter. And Rome was the capital of honor and power. Writing to the people at the center of that world, he begins: I'm not ashamed of this. Notice what he calls the gospel: not an idea or an argument, but power, in Greek dunamis. And notice who it's for: everyone who believes, Jew first and also Greek, no one shut out. Catholics have a small gesture for this. Before the Gospel at Mass, they trace a small cross on the forehead, lips and heart: in my mind, on my lips, in my heart, unashamed.
screen: `A LETTER TO A CHURCH HE'D NEVER SEEN.` · `FIRST IN ORDER, NOT FIRST WRITTEN.` · `A SHAMEFUL DEATH, AN EMBARRASSING MESSAGE.` · `POWER, NOT JUST AN IDEA.` · then, large: `I AM NOT ASHAMED.`

segments.voice: If you pray, picture your next meal with people around, at work or in a cafeteria, and yourself pausing before you eat: a sign of the cross, a few silent words, or a moment of thanks, eyes open. Notice whatever comes up, without judging it. If grace isn't your practice, picture being honest about something you care about, when it would be easier to say not much.
